value.overview: The Worm-eating Warbler (Helmitheros vermivorum) is a small New World wood warbler that breeds in mature deciduous forests of eastern North America and migrates to Central America and northern South America. It is named for its habit of eating caterpillars and other soft-bodied insects rather than worms. In Costa Rica, it is a regular but generally uncommon passage migrant and winter visitor, mainly associated with forested habitats and shaded woodland edges.
value.classification: The Worm-eating Warbler belongs to the family Parulidae, the wood-warblers. It is the only species in the genus Helmitheros.
value.identification: This compact warbler has olive-brown upperparts, buffy or pale underparts, a dark crown marked by two prominent cream-colored stripes, and a narrow dark eye line. It lacks wingbars, helping distinguish it from several similarly colored warblers. The bill is slender and pointed, the tail is short, and the legs are pinkish. It often moves deliberately through dense vegetation or leaf litter and may be easier to detect by its sharp, high-pitched call than by sight.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds from the central and eastern United States south to parts of the southeastern United States. Outside the breeding season it occurs from Mexico through Central America to northern South America. In Costa Rica, it is found mainly during migration and the northern winter, with records from lowland and foothill forests, premontane woodland, shaded edges, second growth, and other habitats with dense leaf cover. It generally favors humid, structurally complex vegetation rather than open agricultural land.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory. Worm-eating Warblers pass through Costa Rica and some remain during the wintering season, especially from roughly September or October through March or April; timing and abundance vary by location and year.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place mainly from April through August in the northern part of the range. The female usually builds a small, cup-shaped nest on or very near the ground, often concealed among dead leaves, grasses, or low vegetation. Two to six eggs are commonly laid, and incubation is performed primarily by the female. Both adults feed the young. Ground nesting makes the species vulnerable to predators and habitat disturbance, but dense forest-floor vegetation provides important concealment.
value.dietFeeding: Worm-eating Warblers feed mainly on caterpillars, moth larvae, beetles, grasshoppers, spiders, and other small arthropods. They commonly search under dead leaves, probe curled leaves, and glean prey from low vegetation and branches. Despite its name, the species does not normally specialize on earthworms. In winter, including in Costa Rica, it continues to forage in dense vegetation and leaf litter within forested habitats.
value.behavior: This warbler is usually quiet and unobtrusive, traveling through dense understory and often keeping close to the ground. It may hop among leaves, climb short distances along branches, or briefly flick its wings while searching for prey. During migration and winter it can occur alone or in mixed-species foraging groups. Males sing most actively on the breeding grounds, while migrants and wintering birds are more often detected by calls and brief views.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered to be declining, with habitat loss and degradation affecting breeding and wintering areas.
conservation.threats: Loss and fragmentation of mature forest, removal of dense understory, and degradation of wintering habitat are important concerns. Because the species nests on or near the ground, it may also be affected by predators, intensive forest-floor management, and disturbance during the breeding season.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect mature forests and connected woodland, retain dense native understory and leaf litter, and limit unnecessary clearing in forest edges and wintering areas. In Costa Rica, conserving humid foothill and lowland forest corridors helps maintain habitat used during migration and winter. Reducing pesticide use can also preserve the insects on which the species depends.
